key_insight: An LLM evaluator can match physician-level agreement on scores, yet still fail to show the clinical caution clinicians use when judging uncertain cases.
clinical_relevance: Automated judges may be useful for scaling medical AI benchmarks, but they need separate checks for abstention behavior and bias before being trusted as stand-ins for clinicians.
method: Built MedQADE, a standardized German open-response clinical benchmark with 3,800 items
Collected annotations from 10 practicing physicians and 9 LLM evaluators
Compared evaluator agreement, abstention behavior, and lineage-dependent bias
evidence_signal: The top evaluator, Gemini 3 Flash, achieved agreement close to the physician ceiling (kappa 0.694 vs. 0.709), but it still gave definitive scores in every case while physicians abstained more on harder items.
watch_item: Statistical agreement alone may hide unsafe evaluator behavior; independence, abstention calibration, and model-lineage bias should be explicitly tested in deployment.
paper_title: Clinician-Level Agreement Without Clinical Caution: LLM Evaluator Limits in Medical AI Benchmarking
